newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Stocks rally in Asia as Fed rate hike fear fades.
newsitem.headline: Stocks rally in Asia as Fed rate hike fear fades.

text.p: Asia stock markets rallied on Monday, inspired by record gains on Wall Street, where expectations were high that the latest batch of U.S. economic data would obviate the need for higher interest rates.
Investors swept into the markets following news of weaker-than-expected gains in both the latest U.S. consumer price index and retail sales.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average gained 67 points on Friday to close at a record of 5,839, and bond prices rallied with the key 30-year government bond gaining nearly 1-1/2 points.
It was the first time the Dow closed above 5,800. The previous record close was 5,778 on May 24.
"The data clearly suggest the Fed does not need to raise interest rates at its upcoming...meeting," said Philip Orlando, chief investment officer at Value Line Asset Management.
The policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) next meets on September 24.

Global financial markets had been awash with speculation that the FOMC would vote to push interest rates higher, based on earlier economic figures that suggested the Fed may raise rates to make a preemptive strike against inflation.
Hong Kong stocks rallied in line with Wall Street, but the key Hang Seng Index ended just short of its 1996 high of 11,600. The index ended up 198.86 points, or 1.75 percent, at 11,567.90.

"The market is actually quite strong all of a sudden. All Asian markets today are a lot better over what is seen as a slightly better interest rate outlook," said James Osborn, sales director at ING Barings.
Tokyo stocks were closed for a public holiday. The key Nikkei 225-share average closed Friday up 398.71 points, or 1.95 percent at 20,842.64.
Philippine shares shot up nearly 40 points, or 1.25 percent, to end at 3,233.67 points, while stocks in Indonesia rose 5.36 points or 0.98 percent to 554.40.
"The Dow's rise on Friday boosted sentiment and prompted the selected blue-chip buying, but volume remained generally moderate," said one broker at a foreign brokerage in Jakarta.

Thai stocks recouped some recent losses and garnered support from purchases of shares by a private fund set up to support the market when prices were depressed. Stocks gained 19.22 points, or 1.85 percent in late afternoon trade, bringing the SET Index to 1,058.87.
The Thai market has been battered in recent weeks due to a variety of economic and political concerns.
Brokers said investors were hopeful that local political problems may ease after a no-confidence motion against Prime Minister Banharn Silpa-archa is debated in parliament on September 18 and 19.
Korean shares gave back early gains and ended basically flat with the composite index up 0.15 points, or 0.02 percent, at 781.88.
Taiwan's weighted index ended up 53.91 points, or 0.83 percent, at 6,518.46.
Malaysia stocks rose sharply on renewed buying interest, and that spilled over to the Singapore market.
"Malaysian stocks are seeing a lot of liquidity, both foreign and speculative funds...largely because some foreign fund manager have re-rated Malaysia," one Singapore dealer said.
The KLSE composite index was up 14.00, or 1.25 percent, at 1,131.55, while Singapore's Straits Times Index was up 28.22 points, or 1.33 percent, at 2,154.49.
Australia's All Ordinaries index ended 15.60 points, or 0.69 percent, higher at 2,267.90.
